tldr: When LLM agents autonomously search for robot control code, combining object-centric physical knowledge, visual scene grounding, and hypothesis-testing experiments enables highly accurate action generation even for complex long-horizon tasks and unseen environments.
hero_caption: The overall framework of RoboAuto. The hierarchical knowledge base on the left maintains object-centric affordances and spatial relations, while scene grounding in the center measures geometric quantities from the current image and connects them to code. The search and exploration module on the right conducts multi-stage planning and active experiments, feeding newly acquired insights back into the knowledge base.
overview:
"Code-as-Policy," where Large Language Models (LLMs) automatically generate and refine robot control programs, is drawing significant attention. However, conventional autonomous agents merely rely on trial-and-error by running programs and fixing code whenever errors appear, without understanding the underlying physical reasons behind "why it failed" or "how this object should be manipulated." Consequently, they frequently make mistakes like knocking over a book by repeatedly trying to grasp it from the top, or swinging in empty air by directly reusing numerical values meant for a mug of a different size.

To address this, the authors propose RoboAuto, a framework in which robots search for programs while understanding physical phenomena across multiple levels. It is built on three core components. First is a hierarchical knowledge base that accumulates "how to handle objects (affordances)," "spatial relations," and "action effects" from video demonstrations and past task-solving experience. Second is scene grounding, which uses vision foundation models such as Molmo2 and SAM 3 to measure critical quantities like grasp poses and object dimensions directly from the current working environment. Third is a hypothesis-driven search mechanism that breaks down the task across physical state changes to verify intermediate stages, running dedicated verification experiments to actively resolve uncertainties whenever the cause of failure is ambiguous.

In evaluation benchmarks, RoboAuto achieved a 73.4% success rate on long-horizon tasks in LIBERO, more than double that of the prior method ASPIRE. Furthermore, it demonstrated exceptional performance across different robot embodiments and simulators, as well as on high-precision real-world cleanup and wiping tasks using a WidowX arm, proving the effectiveness of physical-understanding-based program search.
contributions: Identified fundamental limitations in existing Code-as-Policy methods: lack of physical knowledge, lack of scene grounding, absence of intermediate verification, and lack of active exploration.
Proposed a hierarchical knowledge base that decouples abstract object-centric physical knowledge from executable skills while allowing them to mutually expand each other.
Constructed the RoboAuto search framework, which combines vision-model-driven grounding of scene geometry with stage-by-stage verification and autonomous hypothesis-testing experiments.

Demonstrated substantial performance gains over prior code-search agents and VLA foundation models across five benchmark families and real-robot setups, along with seamless knowledge transfer across simulators and robot embodiments.

sections.heading: Breaking Through the "Physics Wall" Faced by Code-Generating Agents
sections.summary: While robot manipulation through LLM code generation continues to advance, agents often fall into wasteful trial-and-error because they do not understand physical cause-and-effect or object properties. RoboAuto overcomes this barrier by accurately capturing physics at the object, scene, and interaction levels.
sections.details:
Recently, autonomous coding agents powered by LLMs have widely adopted iterative loops of code generation, execution, and refinement to solve problems. In robotics, "Code-as-Policy"—which formulates behaviors as executable programs—has been extensively studied. However, most existing methods rewrite code relying solely on execution errors or binary success/failure feedback, frequently missing the physical root causes of failures.

When observing baseline approaches, the authors identified three typical failure patterns. The first is "insistence on an improper contact strategy." For instance, an agent repeatedly tries to grasp an upright book from above, knocking it down every time. No matter how much the code is patched, it cannot succeed without understanding the object's affordance—that a thin book must be pinched from the sides. The second is "careless reuse of geometric quantities." Applying a grasp height that worked for one mug directly to a different mug causes the gripper to close in empty air. The third is "unverified intermediate states." An agent places a pan on a stove without checking whether turning the burner knob actually succeeded in igniting the flame. Furthermore, when the knob fails to turn, the agent lacks any active experimental means to figure out how many degrees it needs to be rotated.

RoboAuto was developed to resolve these issues. It integrates a knowledge base that decouples object-centric knowledge from executable skills, scene grounding that measures real-time geometric quantities, and a search mechanism that verifies intermediate stage effects while actively testing hypotheses through experiments. As a result, it achieves success rates that substantially surpass prior methods across all benchmarks.

captions.F3: Examples of physical understanding deficits observed in baseline methods. (a) Repeatedly failing to grasp an upright book from above without understanding its affordance, (b) swinging in empty air by directly reusing grasp heights from a different cup, and (c) placing a frying pan onto a stove without verifying whether the burner has ignited.

sections.heading: Foundation Models, Self-Improving Agents, and Where This Work Stands
sections.summary: Robot learning is expanding from early VLA models to Code-as-Policy paradigms. Going beyond parameter updates or simple skill accumulation, this study presents a new paradigm: accumulating and reusing physical understanding itself.
sections.details:
Related work can be categorized into three main areas:

### Robot Foundation Models
Diffusion Policy, large-scale Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models such as OpenVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$, and World-Action Models predicting future observations are advancing rapidly. While these approaches learn direct end-to-end policies from massive datasets, RoboAuto takes a different path by autonomously searching for and refining explicit robot programs. Programmatic representations offer the clear advantages of being human-interpretable, modular, and easy to edit or verify.

### Code-as-Policy and Autonomous Self-Improvement
Prior frameworks include Code-as-Policy, which prompts language models to write programs, ASPIRE, which expands skill libraries from execution histories, and RHO, which iteratively improves policy repositories. However, these systems focus primarily on accumulating and refining prompt templates or raw program code. RoboAuto sets itself apart by maintaining physical knowledge—such as affordances and spatial relations—as an independent foundation and continuously updating it.

### Physical Knowledge and Scene Grounding
Research using knowledge bases in robotics and extracting geometric constraints from 3D scenes is also progressing. RoboAuto achieves flexibility beyond static knowledge retrieval by pairing a grounding mechanism that selectively measures task-critical geometric quantities with an active experimental loop that continuously updates that knowledge.

sections.heading: Understand, Ground, and Experiment: RoboAuto's Three Core Components
sections.summary: RoboAuto comprises three elements: a Hierarchical Knowledge Base, Physical Scene Grounding, and Multi-Stage Planning with Self-Designed Experiments. It organizes knowledge hierarchically, grounds it in current scene measurements, and discovers robust programs through stage-by-stage verification and active experimentation.
sections.details:
RoboAuto's architecture is designed to progressively resolve the physical uncertainties encountered by robots.

### 3.1 Hierarchical Knowledge Base
Knowledge is organized and maintained across two levels of abstraction:
- **Object-Centric Physical Knowledge (High-Level)**: Knowledge that remains independent of specific tasks or concrete programs. It describes affordances, spatial relations, and action effects (e.g., "thin plate-like objects should be pinched from the side," "turning the stove knob ignites the flame"). It contains no low-level control commands or hard-coded coordinates, defining only the measurement procedures for critical geometric quantities (such as opening width or rim radius).
- **Executable Skills (Low-Level)**: Validated program code itself. It includes exact API call patterns, enabling past successful routines to be reused as modular building blocks.

### 3.2 Physical Scene Grounding
This process connects high-level knowledge to the actual scene at hand. Given task instructions and camera observations, it identifies target objects and uses Molmo2 (pointing/referring expression resolution), SAM 3 (segmentation), and depth sensing to measure grasp poses, object dimensions, and orientations. When the initial viewpoint provides insufficient information, it executes active viewpoint selection, moving the robot arm to re-capture clearer observations. This populates the abstract knowledge with concrete, grounded parameters.

### 3.3 Search and Exploration
The task is decomposed across milestones of physical state change and searched stage by stage:
- **Multi-Stage Planning and Grounded Verification**: For each stage, candidate programs and an executable Verifier are generated. The agent never advances to subsequent stages until the current stage passes physical verification. This prevents early errors from cascading into wasteful downstream revisions. Furthermore, to avoid false passes caused by faulty verification code, an Auditor LLM independently evaluates stage outcomes from execution videos and logs.
- **Self-Designed Experiments**: When an execution fails due to physical uncertainty (e.g., "was the grasp pose off, or was the arm reaching its kinematic limit?"), the agent does not restart the entire task. Instead, it autonomously generates and runs isolated micro-experiments to isolate the underlying cause. The resulting findings are immediately incorporated back into the knowledge base.

captions.F13: The search and exploration workflow. The Coder decomposes the task into stages and executes candidate programs alongside verification code (1-2). Upon failure, the Auditor rigorously evaluates the outcome from video footage (3). Once the failing stage is pinpointed (4), the agent autonomously designs and executes isolated experiments to identify the root cause, updating its confidence before refining the code (5).

sections.heading: Outstanding Generalization Proven Across Five Benchmarks and Real Robots
sections.summary: RoboAuto was evaluated across five simulation benchmarks and a real WidowX robotic arm. It achieved more than double ASPIRE's success rate on long-horizon tasks, transferred knowledge seamlessly across simulators and embodiments, and exhibited clear performance scaling as knowledge grew.
sections.details:
The evaluation thoroughly assessed program robustness, long-horizon manipulation, contact-rich control, and cross-robot transferability.

### Primary Benchmark Results
- **LIBERO-PRO Long (Long-Horizon Tasks)**: RoboAuto recorded an average success rate of 73.4%, outperforming the strongest code-search baseline ASPIRE (30.8%) by more than 2x. Stage-by-stage verification proved essential in preventing early failures from propagating downstream.
- **LIBERO-Plus (Viewpoint and Layout Variations)**: Under significant variations in camera angles and scene layouts, ASPIRE achieved only 44.7%, whereas RoboAuto maintained an exceptional 90.3% success rate, demonstrating the power of dynamically measuring values via scene grounding.
- **Robosuite (Contact-Rich Tasks)**: On tasks requiring precise physical contact such as nut assembly, prior baselines struggled below 10%, whereas RoboAuto attained 74% (overall average 90.6% vs. ASPIRE's 81.0%). This confirms that knowledge compiled from LIBERO data transfers effectively to completely different tasks.

### Ablations and Transferability
- **Component Analysis**: The baseline generation loop alone achieved only a 5.2% success rate. Adding multi-stage search and experimentation raised it to 19.2%, incorporating the knowledge base brought it to 38.4%, and finally integrating scene grounding triggered a dramatic surge to 91.2%. Accurately measuring and grounding knowledge in the scene is decisive.
- **Cross-Embodiment Transfer (RoboTwin 2.0)**: Knowledge acquired on a single-arm robot in MuJoCo (LIBERO) was transferred directly to a dual-arm robot in SAPIEN/PhysX. Searching without the knowledge base yielded only 24.5%, whereas applying RoboAuto's knowledge base achieved a remarkable 91.5% success rate.
- **Knowledge Scaling**: As available knowledge base entries were scaled from 0% to 50% and 100%, search efficiency and final success rates exhibited steady and pronounced improvements.

### Real-Robot Experiments
Using a WidowX AI arm, RoboAuto was evaluated on three long-horizon, high-precision tasks: ball sorting, tableware stacking, and whiteboard erasing. Utilizing the knowledge base learned entirely in simulation, RoboAuto achieved nearly flawless stage-completion scores across all tasks. In contrast, ASPIRE stalled mid-execution, and the VLA foundation model $\pi_{0.5}$ (fine-tuned on DROID) failed to complete the tasks.

captions.F8: Execution scenes across three long-horizon real-robot tasks using the WidowX arm. Top row: sorting slippery ping-pong balls; middle row: stacking a plate and a cup; bottom row: erasing whiteboard writing and returning the eraser. Each stage progresses reliably under continuous verification.

sections.heading: Uniting Physical Understanding and Program Search for Autonomous Robotics
sections.summary: By making physical understanding hierarchical, grounded, and testable, RoboAuto substantially elevates the precision and efficiency of autonomous robot program search. Despite practical challenges like physical resets, it marks an important milestone for self-improving robots.
sections.details:
RoboAuto resolves long-standing blind spots in Code-as-Policy by explicitly instilling multi-level physical understanding into LLM agent program search. Its strong empirical performance across both simulation and real-robot setups highlights the complementary relationship between transferable abstract physical knowledge and grounded executable programs.

At the same time, the paper openly discusses current limitations. The primary bottleneck is that autonomous program search remains restricted to simulation environments. When running search on physical robots, resetting object arrangements between trials and monitoring safety still relies on human operators. Integrating automated physical reset mechanisms and safety guardrails will be essential for realizing fully self-evolving robots in the physical world.

sections.heading: Appendix: Deep Dive into Error-Avoidance and Knowledge Base Design
sections.summary: The appendix details case studies illustrating how individual modules alter agent behavior, alongside explicit design guidelines used to keep the knowledge base general and task-agnostic.
sections.details:
The appendix provides in-depth behavioral analyses and implementation details for RoboAuto.

### Behavioral Shifts Across Component Additions
On a long-horizon task involving turning on a stove burner and placing a pan onto it, the authors examine how each component streamlines program search. In the basic loop, the agent had no insight into failure causes and blindly rewrote over 300 lines of code on every attempt. Adding the search module decoupled the "knob turning stage" from the "pan placement stage," successfully localizing edits. Incorporating the knowledge base introduced sound grasp strategies for the knob and handle right from the start. Finally, adding scene grounding allowed the agent to measure the exact knob elevation and pan dimensions, resolving 14 out of 15 scenes in just 36 total trials.

### Rules Enforcing Knowledge Base Generalizability
While the initial knowledge base was constructed from LIBERO-90 videos, strict design rules were enforced to prevent task overfitting or "cheating": (1) no function calls or specific control APIs are included, (2) physical metric values like "3 cm" are strictly excluded in favor of measurement targets, (3) task instruction strings are prohibited, and (4) specific object instance names are replaced with abstract categories such as "slender cylinder" or "hinged door." These four criteria were rigorously validated through both manual inspection and automated pattern checking.

captions.F14: Ablation comparison on the stove-ignition and pan-placement task. The basic loop (top-left) stalls by repeatedly rewriting entire scripts; the search module (top-right) isolates failing stages; the knowledge base (bottom-left) injects viable grasp strategies; and grounding (bottom-right) measures exact dimensions to reach a 92% success rate.

takeaways: To boost Code-as-Policy search efficiency, maintaining abstract physical knowledge—such as object affordances and spatial relationships—is just as vital as refining code syntax.

Rather than hard-coding and reusing past successful values, re-measuring geometric quantities in every environment using vision foundation models (e.g., Molmo2, SAM 3) is key to robust generalization.

Decomposing tasks across physical state transitions for intermediate verification, combined with running dedicated micro-experiments to isolate ambiguous failures, is far more effective than attempting to solve entire tasks in one shot.

Abstract physical knowledge extracted from simulator video demonstrations transfers smoothly across robot embodiments (from single-arm to dual-arm), across different simulation physics engines, and onto physical robots.
limitations: The autonomous program search loop currently relies on simulation, requiring human operators for environment resets and safety monitoring when deployed on real hardware.

Because geometric measurement and intermediate auditing rely on external vision models such as Molmo2 and SAM 3, performance can degrade under challenging visual conditions like severe occlusions, transparent surfaces, or specular reflections.
